content: [b]CenterContainer[/b] is a container that keeps all of its child controls in its center at their minimum size.

A container that keeps its child controls within the area of a [url]StyleBox^^https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_stylebox.html#class-stylebox[/url]. Useful for giving controls an outline.

A variant of [url]BoxContainer^^https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_boxcontainer.html#class-boxcontainer[/url] that can only arrange its child controls horizontally or vertically. Child controls are rearranged automatically when their minimum size changes.
A Theme is a resource used for styling/skinning Controls and Windows. Create your own Theme instead of adding Theme Overrides on individual Control Nodes.

When designing a user interface there may be times when a Control node needs to have a different look than what is normally defined by a Theme. Every control node has theme property overrides, which allow you to redefine the styling for each individual UI element.

To create a type variation open the theme editor, then click the plus icon next to the [b]Type[/b] dropdown on the right side of the editor. Type in what you want to name your theme type variation in the text box, then click [b]Add Type[/b].
Below the [b]Type[/b] dropdown are the property tabs. Switch to the tab with a wrench and screwdriver icon.

Click on the plus icon next to the Base Type field. You can select the base type there, which would typically be the name of a control node class (e.g., [k]Button[/k], [k]Label[/k], etc). Type variations can also chain and extend other type variations. This works in the same way control nodes inherit styling of their base class. For example, [k]CheckButton[/k] inherits styles from[k]Button[/k] because corresponding node types extend each other.
After you select the base type, you should now be able to see its properties on the other tabs in the theme editor. You can edit them as usual.

Now that a type variation has been created you can apply it to your nodes. In the inspector dock, under the [b]Theme[/b] property of a control node, you can find the [b]Theme Type Variation[/b] property. It is empty by default, which means that only the base type has an effect on this node.

You can either select a type variation from a dropdown list, or input its name manually. Variations appear on the list only if the type variation belongs to the project-wide theme, which you can configure in the project settings. For any other case you have to input the name of the variation manually. Click on the pencil icon to the right. Then type in the name of the type variation and click the check mark icon or press enter. If a type variation with that name exists it will now be used by the node.,
An empty StyleBox that can be used to display nothing instead of the default style (e.g. it can "disable" [k]focus[/k] styles). StyleBoxEmpty gives you nothing but padding.
By configuring various properties of this style box, you can achieve many common looks without the need of a texture. This includes optionally rounded borders, antialiasing, shadows, and skew.
Setting corner radius to high values is allowed. As soon as corners overlap, the stylebox will switch to a relative system
A StyleBox that displays a single line of a given color and thickness. The line can be either horizontal or vertical. Useful for separators.

A texture-based nine-patch StyleBox, in a way similar to [url]NinePatchRect^^https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_ninepatchrect.html#class-ninepatchrect[/url]. This stylebox performs a 3×3 scaling of a texture, where only the center cell is fully stretched. This makes it possible to design bordered styles regardless of the stylebox's size.

key_concepts: In this tutorial, we will be creating an interface or component setup to add animations to the UI, which will be easier than creating a script for every single node we want to animate.

We can delete the _process() function, and add two tween functions; one for when we hover onto the button, and another for when we hover off. We will also add a function for creating the tweens:
In the code above, the [i]add_tween()[/i] method is used to add tween animations to a node. The [i]on_hover()[/i] method adds a tween when the [i]target[/i] is hovered.
Now we need to finish setting things up:

In the [i]_ready()[/i] method connects the two tween functions to the target hover functions. The [i]setup()[/i] method finishes configuring the component with the target's transform behaviour and default scale. It has to be called using [i]call_deferred()[/i] since if it's called too early, the target Node's pivot and scale won't be set until all its children are ready.

This is the beginning of an animation framework that can be used for UI elements, such as buttons, labels, panels, etc... Play with the current setup on a set of buttons to see how you prefer to use it.

key_concepts: In this tutorial, we will be implementing multiple animations on Control nodes so that the animations can occur either simultaneously or sequentially.

content: Since we will want to animate several properties at a time we will need to capture those values in export variables. Add the following export variables to the class definition:

In the above code, we added the [i]export_group[/i] property to group the export values together in the Editor, and added several new fields to capture and a dictionary to store them in. These can be set in the Editor now to apply to the "Hover" animation.
The values above cover changes applied when the target is being hovered, but we also need to capture the default values to return to when hovering stops. We will capture them in the following code:

In the above code we create a list of properties to capture and a dictionary to store them in, as well as a flags for performing the transforms from the center and running them in parallel. When we need to capture the default values, we will do so from the [b]setup()[/b] method, since it is run after all UI nodes are ready.

With the correct values stored in our dictionaries, we will want to change the way we add the tweens. We will want to set whether the animations play in parallel, and set each animation in order. The code below does this:
We will also want to change where the signal connections are made, so add them to the end of the [i]setup()[/i] method:

content.code:
target.mouse_entered.connect(add_tween.bind(
		hover_values,
		run_parallel_animations,
		hover_duration,
		hover_transition_type,
		hover_easing,
	))
	target.mouse_exited.connect(add_tween.bind(
		default_values,
		run_parallel_animations,
		hover_duration,
		hover_transition_type,

key_concepts: In this tutorial, we will be adding the ability to delay animations in the UiAnimationNode. To do this, we will add a new export property to the [b]Hover Settings[/b] group: [b]hover_delay: float[/b].

Now when we run the [i]add_tween()[/i] method, we want to add a pause after setting the parallel flag before adding properties, and then add a timeout before playing the tween. the new [i]add_tween()[/i] code is below:
In this tutorial, we will be creating an animation when first loading Control nodes, such as having a menu popup or fade in.

content: First, we will want to add several new settings for entrance animations. First, we want a flag indicating whether the animation is for an entrance animation, and then we will want to create an export group for those values. Just copy-paste the hover settings and rename all the values:

content.code:
## Runs the initial setup to capture default and hover animation property values.
func setup() -> void:
	if from_center:
		target.pivot_offset = target.size * 0.5

	default_values = {
		"scale": target.scale,
		"position": target.position,
		"rotation": target.rotation,
		"size": target.size,
		"self_modulate": target.modulate
	}

	entrance_values = {
		"scale": entrance_scale,
		"position": target.position + entrance_position,
		"rotation": target.rotation + deg_to_rad(entrance_rotation),
		"size": target.size + entrance_size,
		"self_modulate": entrance_modulate
	}

	hover_values = {
		"scale": hover_scale,
		"position": target.position + hover_position,
		"rotation": target.rotation + deg_to_rad(hover_rotation),
		"size": target.size + hover_size,
		"self_modulate": hover_modulate
	}
	target.mouse_entered.connect(add_tween.bind(
		hover_values,
		run_parallel_animations,
		hover_duration,
		hover_delay,
		hover_transition_type,
		hover_easing,
	))
	target.mouse_exited.connect(add_tween.bind(
		default_values,
		run_parallel_animations,
		hover_duration,
		hover_delay,
		hover_transition_type,
		hover_easing,
	))

	if is_entrance_animation:
		on_entrance()


func on_entrance() -> void:
	add_tween(
		entrance_values,
		true,
		0.0,
		0.0,
		IMMEDIATE_TRANSITION,
		entrance_easing,
	)
	add_tween(
		default_values,
		run_parallel_animations,
		entrance_duration,
		entrance_delay,
		entrance_transition_type,
		entrance_easing,
	)

content: In [i]setup()[/i] we added a call to a new function, [i]on_entrance()[/i]. This runs if the animation is marked as an entrance animation.

Let's say you want one node's entrance animation to play after another node's animations have finished.  We will add an export variable to the [b]Entrance Animation Settings[/b] to capture the node that should be watched.

content.code:
## the UiAnimationNode that plays immediately before this
@export var wait_for: UiAnimationNode

content: In order to know when a node's animation is finished, we can create a signal for that.

content.code:
## signal that the entrance animation has finished
signal entrance_animation_finished

content: We can emit this signal in places when it is done, such as in [i]setup()[/i] when there is no entrance animation, or at the end of [i]add_tween()[/i]. We also add another parameter to [i]add_tween()[/i] to indicate when an entrance animation is playing.
Last, you will need to connect the signal emission to a call to [i]add_tween()[/i]. Do this in the [i]setup()[/i] after making your connections:

content.code:
## Runs the initial setup to capture default and hover animation property values.
func setup() -> void:
	if from_center:
		target.pivot_offset = target.size * 0.5

	default_values = {
		"scale": target.scale,
		"position": target.position,
		"rotation": target.rotation,
		"size": target.size,
		"self_modulate": target.modulate
	}

	entrance_values = {
		"scale": entrance_scale,
		"position": target.position + entrance_position,
		"rotation": target.rotation + deg_to_rad(entrance_rotation),
		"size": target.size + entrance_size,
		"self_modulate": entrance_modulate
	}

	hover_values = {
		"scale": hover_scale,
		"position": target.position + hover_position,
		"rotation": target.rotation + deg_to_rad(hover_rotation),
		"size": target.size + hover_size,
		"self_modulate": hover_modulate
	}
	target.mouse_entered.connect(add_tween.bind(
		hover_values,
		run_parallel_animations,
		hover_duration,
		hover_delay,
		hover_transition_type,
		hover_easing,
	))
	target.mouse_exited.connect(add_tween.bind(
		default_values,
		run_parallel_animations,
		hover_duration,
		hover_delay,
		hover_transition_type,
		hover_easing,
	))
	if wait_for:
		wait_for.entrance_animation_finished.connect(add_tween.bind(
			default_values,
			run_parallel_animations,
			entrance_duration,
			entrance_delay,
			entrance_transition_type,
			entrance_easing,
			true
		))

	if is_entrance_animation:
		on_entrance()
	else:
		entrance_animation_finished.emit()
